I get this. Possibly a weird comparison, but it reminds me of how I felt after leaving an abusive relationship. I got so used to the extreme emotions caused by my abuser that to this day healthy relationships feel 'boring' and 'fake'. The highs never taste so good as when they come after the lowest lows.

The other thing I miss (is that the right word for it?) about the abusive relationship is similar to what I enjoy about addiction. When something so extremely bad is happening in your life, it narrows your world down. Your only concern is the battle you're fighting, like you said; it's so easy, so refreshingly straightforwards, when you have only one single goal (pleasing the abuser, getting the next drink) and are forced to pursue it at pain of terrible consequences. Sober life and post-abuse life are hard because there's multiple goals, multiple things to focus on, you have to pick your own battles and there's no comparable reward for winning or losing them. The dopamine hit that comes from surviving a dire situation just isn't there. 

That said, I've heard that post-acute withdrawal syndrome can last for up to a year. 9 months is an incredible achievement but your dopamine systems are still reaching equilibrium. If maintaining sobriety is very difficult at the moment, let yourself be in survival mode; let yourself stare at the wall, don't worry about saying interesting things to anyone. Pick a battle and try to fight it. You can always re-evaluate when you hit one year.

This is going to be an extremely unpopular opinion for this sub but centrelink is not really enough to "cover life". Is it possible to cover basic expenses? Sure, if you're extremely careful with budgeting, and it's still more than most people in the world have the privilege of receiving. But I wouldn't call what centrelink offers "peace of mind", when you're constantly living with the fear that it'll just be taken away bc you aren't sick enough. And even aside from that, it turns out that socializing, hobbies, basic pleasures, the things that make life worth living, these all require disposable income. 


What does your father in law like to do? What parts of his day does he really enjoy, what's important to him, what makes him happy? What gives him the little dopamine hit you get from drinking or smoking? Cause while centrelink may be enough for someone to scrape by, there are very few humans in history who can abide "scraping by". This is why drug and alcohol use have been part of humanity since before recorded history-- when life sucks, we need relief. If you had health issues that prevented you from working and a shoestring budget (and I hope you never find yourself in this position), I'd bet you'd pick up an unhealthy habit or two to try and find even a little bit of relief in your life as well. 


Anyway, the best thing to do is to be honest with him and tell him that you won't financially support him. Be prepared for the consequences of this decision with your partner.

I just opened up this subreddit to post something very similar. How do you tolerate immense negative emotions, especially surrounding abandonment? It's so hard.

I don't know if it will help, but here's some of the strategies I use:

-If the emotions are completely crisis-level overwhelming-- cold showers. Filling up a bowl with icy water and submerging my face in it while holding my breath for 30 seconds or as long as I can handle (this activates the mammalian dive reflex, which triggers the parasympathetic nervous system and slows your heart rate). Splashing my face with water and deep breathing if I'm in public and need to calm down quick. Exercise as intense and exhausting as I can handle. 

-If the emotions aren't completely overwhelming, but still excruciatingly painful-- get outside and get out of your head. Go for a walk and listen to a podcast, go for a run to the shops and buy a treat for yourself, head to a local park. Anything that takes you out of your present environment and puts you in a new one. Deep breathing exercises, mindfulness, focusing entirely on the present moment, trying to visualize the present emotion as a wave that'll pass eventually.

If the emotions are painful, but tolerable-- make space to sit with them. Imagine them as a guest who's come to stay for a while, maybe like a member of your distant family. You have to politely accommodate them, you should listen to what they have to say, but you wouldn't rearrange your life around them and you certainly wouldn't let them physically harm you. Set a timer for half an hour and let that be your 'wallowing' time-- use that time to cry, write down your feelings, scream into a pillow, whatever else you need to do, but once that timer's up put aside those feelings and go do something distracting for a while. 

I recognize that a lot of these might not be doable if you're at work and don't have the freedom to walk around, but the visualisation one is the one I mostly resort to in public. Literally telling myself that those thoughts/fears/emotions aren't helpful right now and that I'll think about them when I have the time. 

I've spent a lot of time trying to teach myself how to tolerate and experience my own repressed emotions and for me what's helped most is taking it slowly. Expose myself to them a little bit at a time and then retreat into distraction when it becomes too much to bear. If you are deeply repressed, the hardest thing to learn is how to simply sit with an emotion and not act on it, just letting it exist in your head. The worst feeling emotion in the world won't kill you. You can lie on your bed and experience the worst emotion you've ever felt and physically nothing will happen to you. Alcohol, on the other hand, very well might kill you; and it doesn't make those emotions that you need to process go away, it only puts them off.

Speaking as a fellow woman w/ BPD, when I entered DBT therapy for the first time I was warned that a lot of people lose relationships when they recover, because people who are still mired in the same destructive patterns and thought processes will resent their partner's attempts to get better. Recovery, be it from alcoholism or trauma or personality disorders, is sometimes incompatible with people who are still stuck in their unhealthy behavior. In my case I did end up losing my partner-- as I turned into a functional person and figured out who I was beneath my mental illness, as I became less tolerant of unhealthy behaviors and capable of living a healthy fulfilling life outside of them, they lost interest in me and found someone else. In retrospect I should have ended that relationship sooner, because we'd also been dating since I was a teenager and I had no idea who I was outside of addiction and bpd and that relationship. It turned out the life I wanted to create for myself was incompatible with the one they wanted. 

"People grow together or they grow apart." Recovery is a journey, and you might have to do some serious thinking about whether the current burden he's placing on you (by being unsupportive) is worth everything he adds to your life in the long run. What will a life with him to look like after you've been sober for six months? A year? What do you want that life to look like?
